text: My flatmate balanced his coffee on my laptop while streaming a match, and of course it tipped over the keyboard. He said it was only a laptop and went back to his phone. I stood there with trembling hands, ready to say things I couldn't take back.

The ration shop clerk kept sending my father to the back of the line because he can't read the English form. Dad is seventy-three and stood two hours in the heat. I wanted to shout at the entire counter.
The cast list for the school play goes up on the notice board after lunch. I've been walking past that corridor all morning pretending not to look. Any minute now I'll know.
The ferry to Elephanta runs again from next week and I've promised my nephew a ride. He has already drawn the boat in his notebook, with us waving from the deck. We're counting the days together.
The cab seat was sticky and someone had left chewed gum on the door handle. The driver kept spitting out of the window as we moved. I sat on the very edge of the seat for the whole ride.
A cockroach crawled out of my tiffin box when I opened it at my desk. I dropped the lid and pushed the whole thing to the far corner. I couldn't look at lunch for the rest of the day.
The lift stopped between floors and the lights flickered off. Someone's phone torch was the only light. I counted my breaths and tried not to think of how small the space was.
My daughter hasn't replied to any message since morning and her phone goes straight to voicemail. I keep imagining roads and hospitals. My hands won't stop shaking as I redial.
My painting got picked for the district exhibition! I read the email on the bus and nearly shouted. The conductor asked if I'd won a lottery and I said, something like that.
It rained on our rooftop picnic and nobody cared. We ate maggi out of steel bowls and sang old songs until the thunder joined in. I haven't felt this light since school.
Every morning he leaves a tiny sticky note on my lunch box with a terrible pun. I keep them all in a drawer. I would choose this man a thousand times over.
My mother-in-law taught me her mustard fish recipe today, patiently, three times over. She wiped my sleeve when the oil splashed. I felt truly welcomed into the family, and it filled me with warmth.
The prototype failed again, but this time we know exactly which part broke. One redesign and the next test should hold. I really think we're close.
The new coach is strict, but the team's fitness is already better. If we keep training like this, next season could be our best yet. I'm confident about where we're headed.
They say airfares will drop next year, but they always say that. Prices only ever go one way. I've stopped checking the fare tracker altogether.
This is our third pitch to the same client, who rejected the last two for the same reasons. We've changed nothing meaningful. I'm sure we'll hear no again.

The shelf of my brother's trophies still gets dusted every Sunday, though he's been abroad for two years. Mum never says anything, just wipes each one slowly. I stood in the doorway and felt the distance in my chest.
My cat didn't come when I called this morning. The vet said it was kidney failure and that nothing more could be done. I held her till the end and haven't stopped crying since.
I checked my bank app and saw a refund I had stopped expecting a year ago. I blinked at the screen three times, then showed it to my mother. We both just stared.

I let my nephew drive the car back, though he has only had his licence a month. He's careful about the small things and I've watched him grow into someone responsible. I fell asleep in the passenger seat without a worry.
Tomorrow I'll meet my biological father for the first time. I've wanted this for years and can't wait to hear his voice. But I keep wondering if he'll like me, and my stomach is in a knot.

My manager gave the project credit to someone who joined last month. I was furious in the meeting, but in the washroom afterwards I just cried. Two years of late nights, and that was all it counted for.
Our anniversary dinner was nothing fancy, just rajma chawal on the balcony. She laughed at my bad jokes and held my hand under the table. I felt completely in love and completely happy.
I opened an old tiffin I'd forgotten in my bag and a cloud of fruit flies flew out. I yelped and jumped back. I had no idea anything could rot that fast, and the smell clung to me for hours.
My CA told me the audit will be fine and I believe him; he has never got a number wrong. I'm calm about next week. I even think we might get a refund.
Grandma's sari still smells of her talcum powder. I wrapped it around my shoulders and sat on her bed. I miss her badly, and I feel so much love for her that it hurts.

Someone tried my car door handle at midnight outside our gate. I locked the doors with shaking hands, then felt angry that I can't even park safely in my own building. I called the guard and shouted at him.
She cleared the final trials and was selected for the national team. We all cheered, and Mum kept wiping her eyes. We're so proud, but it also means she'll be away for most of the year.
The new puppy comes home on Sunday. I've bought a tiny bed and three chew toys, and I giggle every time I look at them. It's going to be such a good week.
The ministry has postponed the exam date a fourth time. I'm furious that they treat students like this, and I don't believe they will ever announce a fair timetable. Why should I keep preparing?
I was terrified as the cab drove through the flooded underpass and the water rose to the doors. We came out the other side and the driver turned around grinning. We both whooped like kids.

The first week in the hostel was lonely and I called home every night in tears. By the third week I had a group to eat with and a corner of the library that felt like mine. Now I laugh at how scared I was.
I stormed to the neighbour's door, ready to yell about the noise. A little girl answered and told me her mother was in hospital. My anger just drained away and I felt awful.
I'd saved my appetite for the famous kachori at the highway stop. It arrived greasy and cold, with a fly walking across the chutney. I couldn't manage more than one bite.
I began the year sure I'd finish my novel by June. By September I had four chapters and no plot. Now I doubt it will ever be done.
I opened an old library book and found a ten-rupee note with a message from some stranger saying to buy myself chai. I stared at it, then grinned. It made my whole afternoon.

I'd never flown with a baby and I was shaking as we boarded. The air hostess took one look and offered to warm the milk, and a stranger across the aisle held our bag. By landing I felt we'd been looked after the whole way.
We were laughing over biryani at a new place when the bill came with a service charge nobody had mentioned. The waiter refused to remove it. The evening soured and I was still fuming in the auto.
The studio rejected my script and I walked home in silence. At night I reread it and realised the second act really was weak. I opened the laptop to fix it, feeling oddly hopeful.
The durian smell hit me at the door and I covered my nose. But the first taste was creamy and sweet, and I was stunned. I never expected to like it.
I'm not angry that she left without saying goodbye. I'm only quietly sad that the friendship ended so softly. Nobody did anything wrong, and that makes it harder.
It isn't relief that the exam is over, exactly. It's more that I'm just happy to have time for painting again. I spent the whole evening mixing colours and humming.
I'm not nervous about the speech itself, it's the questions after it that keep me up. What if someone asks something I can't answer?
Nobody has promised us anything, but I'm not discouraged. The small signs are good and I think the next quarter will be better. I'm hopeful.
I'm not worried about handing him the project. He hasn't missed a deadline in three years and doesn't need checking. I'll sleep well tonight.
Took the 9:05 bus to the bank and waited in the second queue. Deposited the cheque, collected the receipt, and updated the passbook. Then I walked to the stationery shop next door.
Cut the vegetables for sambar, put the pressure cooker on, and set the table. Dinner was ready by eight. I washed the pots and left the rice container to dry.
The water tank will be cleaned on Wednesday between nine and noon. Please store water in advance. The secretary has put up a notice near the lifts.
Charged my phone, packed my headphones, and checked the calendar for tomorrow. There is a standup at ten and a review at three. I set the laptop bag by the door.
Went to the gym at six, did half an hour on the treadmill and some stretches, and showered. Back home by seven for breakfast.
